text: TLS already showed up earlier in this catalog — the handshake, the session key, the certificate behind the padlock. This lesson looks at how that exact protocol gets applied in a cloud environment specifically: what traffic it covers, and the real defaults Azure and AWS now enforce instead of leaving TLS optional.

In the cloud, TLS does double duty. It secures traffic between a client — a browser, a script, an app — and a cloud service, and it secures traffic between cloud services talking to each other behind the scenes, like a web app calling a database or a storage account. Every network hop, whether it crosses the public internet or stays entirely inside the provider's own network, is a hop TLS needs to cover.

Azure Storage Accounts enable Secure transfer required by default on new accounts — any plain HTTP request gets rejected outright, not just discouraged. Amazon S3 lets you enforce the same behavior with a bucket policy that denies any request where aws:SecureTransport is false. Both platforms have moved from 'TLS is available if you set it up' to 'TLS is required unless you deliberately turn it off,' a meaningful shift from how cloud storage defaults used to work.

Using 'TLS' isn't enough on its own — old versions, TLS 1.0 and 1.1, have known weaknesses and are considered insecure today. Azure and AWS both now enforce a minimum TLS version across most managed services, TLS 1.2 at minimum with TLS 1.3 increasingly supported, and a connection trying to negotiate an older version gets refused rather than silently downgraded.

Every TLS connection still needs a certificate binding a public key to an identity. In the cloud, that certificate typically comes from Azure Key Vault, which stores certificates alongside keys and secrets, or AWS Certificate Manager, AWS's dedicated service for issuing and renewing TLS certificates. Centralizing issuance there means renewals happen automatically instead of a certificate quietly expiring and taking a production service down.
Encryption at rest and in transit both still depend on one thing: a secret — a key, a connection string, an API token — staying out of the wrong hands. Next up: why you never hardcode a secret.
